mean: may everything go as you wish (a greeting)
lit: ten thousand things, all as you wish

use.how: A set wish, said alone or after 祝你/祝您: 祝您新年快乐，万事如意！ Used at New Year, birthdays and in cards; also in 人生哪能万事如意.

near.diff: 一路顺风 wishes someone a safe journey only; 万事如意 wishes that everything in life goes well.
一帆风顺 is smooth progress in one undertaking or career; 万事如意 is the all-round greeting for every part of life.

cue: You are writing a New Year card to your old teacher and want to wish them well in every part of life. How do you end it?

ctx.s: 新年快乐，祝您身体健康，{万事如意}！
ctx.en: Happy New Year! Wishing you good health and that everything goes your way!

ctx.s: 奶奶过生日，我们一起举杯，祝她老人家{万事如意}。
ctx.en: At Grandma's birthday we all raised our glasses and wished her every happiness.

ctx.s: 贺卡最后，他写了一句：“祝阿姨{万事如意}，天天开心！”
ctx.en: At the end of the card he wrote: "Wishing you all the best, Auntie, and happiness every day!"

ctx.s: 春节拜年的时候，大家见面总要说一句“{万事如意}”。
ctx.en: When people pay New Year visits at Spring Festival, they always greet each other with "may all go well".

ctx.s: 婚礼上，主持人祝新郎新娘白头偕老、{万事如意}。
ctx.en: At the wedding the host wished the bride and groom a long life together and every happiness.

ctx.s: “祝你工作顺利，家庭幸福，{万事如意}！”“谢谢，也祝你全家都好！”
ctx.en: "Wishing you success at work, a happy family and all the best in everything!" "Thanks, and all the best to your whole family too!"

bad.s: 他这次考试{万事如意}，得了满分。
bad.en: (meant: his exam went smoothly and he got full marks)
bad.why: The first half means everything in life; it is a broad wish, not a report that one event went well. Say the exam went smoothly instead.

bad.s: 祝你{万事如意}地通过考试。
bad.en: (meant: I hope you pass the exam smoothly)
bad.why: It is a complete wish on its own, not an adverb for a verb. Wish someone a smooth pass in plain words, or use the idiom by itself.

mean: fully willing, gladly accepting it of one's own accord
lit: the heart content and the feelings willing

use.how: Adverbial (心甘情愿地做) or predicate (我是心甘情愿的). Stresses that a cost, hardship or sacrifice is accepted freely, without being forced.

near.diff: 一厢情愿 is one side's wishful thinking that ignores the other side; 心甘情愿 is freely accepting a cost yourself.

cue: A friend pities you for spending every weekend caring for your sick father. You say nobody forced you: you choose to do it.

ctx.s: 为了孩子，妈妈{心甘情愿}地吃苦。
ctx.en: For her children's sake, the mother willingly puts up with hardship.

ctx.s: 这份工作工资不高，但他做得{心甘情愿}。
ctx.en: The job doesn't pay much, but he does it gladly.

ctx.s: “你周末还去医院照顾爸爸，不累吗？”“累，但我是{心甘情愿}的。”
ctx.en: "You go to the hospital to look after your dad even at weekends. Aren't you tired?" "I am, but I do it willingly."

ctx.s: 没有人逼他，他是{心甘情愿}捐出这笔钱的。
ctx.en: Nobody pressured him; he donated the money entirely of his own accord.

ctx.s: 这是我自己选的路，再苦再累我也{心甘情愿}。
ctx.en: This is the path I chose myself; however hard and tiring it gets, I accept it gladly.

ctx.s: 合同的条件很苛刻，可她为了这个机会，还是{心甘情愿}地签了字。
ctx.en: The terms of the contract were harsh, but for the sake of the opportunity she signed it willingly.

bad.s: 她{心甘情愿}他明天来。
bad.en: (meant: she is happy for him to come tomorrow)
bad.why: It describes one's own readiness to do or bear something; it cannot take another person's action as its object, the way 'hope' can.

bad.s: 他{心甘情愿}地以为她也喜欢他。
bad.en: (meant: he fondly imagined that she liked him too)
bad.why: Believing what you wish were true is wishful thinking, a different idiom. This one means freely accepting a cost yourself.

lit: mountains of people, seas of people

use.how: Predicate or attributive with 的, describing a place packed with people: 广场上人山人海。 It paints a scene; it does not count things.

near.diff: 成千上万 gives a large number of anything (people, letters, birds); 人山人海 pictures one place packed with a crowd.

cue: On the first day of the national holiday you reach a famous scenic spot and can barely move for the crowds. How do you describe it?

ctx.s: 国庆节的时候，长城上{人山人海}。
ctx.en: During the National Day holiday the Great Wall is packed with people.

ctx.s: 演唱会门口{人山人海}，我们根本挤不进去。
ctx.en: There was a sea of people at the concert entrance; we couldn't squeeze in at all.

ctx.s: “周末去公园吗？”“算了吧，肯定{人山人海}。”
ctx.en: "Shall we go to the park this weekend?" "Forget it, it'll be heaving with people."

ctx.s: 春运期间，火车站里{人山人海}，到处都是拿着行李的旅客。
ctx.en: During the Spring Festival travel rush the station is a sea of people, with travellers and luggage everywhere.

ctx.s: 早知道商场打折时{人山人海}，我就不来了。
ctx.en: If I'd known the mall would be this packed during the sale, I wouldn't have come.

ctx.s: 记者站在{人山人海}的广场上，报道新年倒计时的盛况。
ctx.en: Standing in the packed square, the reporter described the grand New Year countdown.

bad.s: 我们班有{人山人海}的学生。
bad.en: (meant: our class has a great many students)
bad.why: It pictures a crowd packed into one place, not the number of members in a group. Simply say the class has many students.

bad.s: 我家的书{人山人海}，书架都放不下了。
bad.en: (meant: we have so many books the shelves can't hold them)
bad.why: It is only about crowds of people. For a great many things, use an ordinary 'very many' or a different image.

mean: to fall in love at first sight
lit: at one look, the feelings gather on someone

use.how: Predicate, often 对某人一见钟情, or attributive (一见钟情的爱情). Mainly about romantic love; playfully also about an object you love at once.

near.diff: 青梅竹马 is a bond that grew from childhood together; 一见钟情 is love that strikes at the very first meeting.

cue: Your friend met someone at a wedding, talked for five minutes, and has thought of nobody else since. How did it start?

ctx.s: 他在图书馆遇见了她，就{一见钟情}了。
ctx.en: He met her in the library and fell for her at first sight.

ctx.s: 你相信{一见钟情}吗？
ctx.en: Do you believe in love at first sight?

ctx.s: 我父母是在火车上认识的，爸爸对妈妈{一见钟情}。
ctx.en: My parents met on a train; my dad fell in love with my mum the moment he saw her.

ctx.s: 这部电影讲的是两个陌生人在雨中{一见钟情}的故事。
ctx.en: The film is about two strangers who fall in love at first sight in the rain.

ctx.s: 这套房子我一走进去就{一见钟情}，当天就交了定金。
ctx.en: I fell in love with this flat the moment I walked in and paid the deposit that same day.

ctx.s: 与其说是{一见钟情}，不如说是日久生情，他们做了三年同事才在一起。
ctx.en: It wasn't so much love at first sight as love that grew over time: they were colleagues for three years before getting together.

bad.s: 我和他认识十年了，慢慢地{一见钟情}。
bad.en: (meant: over ten years I gradually fell in love with him)
bad.why: It means love at the very first meeting, so it cannot happen slowly over ten years. For love that grows over time, use another phrase.

bad.s: 我第一次见到新老板就{一见钟情}，觉得他很能干。
bad.en: (meant: my first impression of the new boss was that he is very capable)
bad.why: It means falling in love, not forming a good opinion of someone. For a good first impression of a boss, say that plainly.

lit: to 'eat' one big shock: the word for 'be startled' split open by 'big' and 'one'

use.how: Predicate (他大吃一惊) or after 让/令 (这个消息让我大吃一惊). A sudden strong surprise at unexpected news or a sight, good or bad; takes no object.

near.diff: 目瞪口呆 shows the frozen, speechless look of someone stunned; 大吃一惊 simply names the strong surprise.
喜出望外 is delight at unexpected good news; 大吃一惊 is strong surprise at anything, good or bad.

cue: You check the restaurant bill and find it is three times what you expected. What is your reaction?

ctx.s: 听到这个消息，我{大吃一惊}。
ctx.en: I was astonished when I heard the news.

ctx.s: 他打开门，看见满屋子的朋友，{大吃一惊}。
ctx.en: He opened the door, saw a room full of friends and got the shock of his life.

ctx.s: 成绩一向很差的小明这次考了第一名，让老师{大吃一惊}。
ctx.en: Xiaoming, whose marks had always been poor, came first this time, which greatly surprised the teacher.

ctx.s: 医生看了检查结果，{大吃一惊}，马上让他住院。
ctx.en: The doctor was alarmed by the test results and had him admitted to hospital at once.

ctx.s: 结账时一看账单，我们都{大吃一惊}：一顿饭竟然花了这么多钱。
ctx.en: When we saw the bill we were all stunned: one meal had cost that much.

ctx.s: 这家小公司的产品卖到了全世界，令同行{大吃一惊}。
ctx.en: This small company's products are now sold worldwide, much to the astonishment of its rivals.

bad.s: 他从小就{大吃一惊}，什么都怕。
bad.en: (meant: he has been timid since childhood and is afraid of everything)
bad.why: It is one moment of shock at something unexpected, not a lasting timid character. Say he has always been easily scared.

bad.s: 我{大吃一惊}了这个消息。
bad.en: (meant: I was shocked by this news)
bad.why: It takes no object. Put the news first as the cause (on hearing the news, I was...) or make the news the subject with 'made me'.

lit: a thousand methods and a hundred schemes

use.how: Adverbial before the verb it serves: 千方百计地想办法, 千方百计逃避责任. Stresses trying method after method, for good aims or bad ones.

near.diff: 全力以赴 is throwing all one's strength into one task; 千方百计 is trying one method after another to reach a goal.

cue: A boy wants a puppy: he begs, writes letters, offers to do chores and even gets his grandparents to ask. How does he go about it?

ctx.s: 孩子生病了，父母{千方百计}地给他找好医生。
ctx.en: When their child fell ill, the parents tried everything to find him a good doctor.

ctx.s: 为了让我答应，他{千方百计}地讨好我。
ctx.en: To get me to say yes, he tried every way he could think of to please me.

ctx.s: 那只猫{千方百计}想从笼子里跑出来。
ctx.en: The cat tried every trick it could to get out of the cage.

ctx.s: 他{千方百计}逃避责任，最后还是被发现了。
ctx.en: He tried every possible way to dodge responsibility, but in the end he was found out.

ctx.s: 公司正在{千方百计}降低成本，连办公室的灯都少开了。
ctx.en: The company is cutting costs by every means it can; even the office lights are switched on less.

ctx.s: “你们是怎么找到这本旧书的？”“我们{千方百计}地打听，问遍了全城的旧书店。”
ctx.en: "How did you find this old book?" "We asked around every way we could and tried every second-hand bookshop in the city."

bad.s: 这个问题很简单，我{千方百计}就解决了。
bad.en: (meant: the problem was simple and I solved it right away)
bad.why: It implies great trouble and many attempts, so it cannot describe something easy that was done at once.

bad.s: 明天就是决赛了，大家一定要{千方百计}！
bad.en: (meant: the final is tomorrow, everyone must give it their all!)
bad.why: It needs the action it serves after it (by every means, win the match). As a standalone rallying call to give everything, use the 'go all out' idiom.

mean: to go all out, putting everything into it
lit: to set off toward it with all one's strength

use.how: Predicate, often after 要/会/一定: 我们会全力以赴。 Said of a serious task, match or emergency; a pledge of total effort. Takes no object.

near.diff: 尽力而为 is a modest 'I'll do what I can' that leaves room for failure; 全力以赴 pledges everything.
千方百计 is trying many different methods, even to dodge something; 全力以赴 is wholehearted effort on one worthy task.

cue: Before the final, the coach asks whether the team is ready. The captain promises they will hold nothing back.

ctx.s: 明天的比赛，我们一定{全力以赴}。
ctx.en: In tomorrow's match we'll give it everything we've got.

ctx.s: 地震发生后，救援人员{全力以赴}抢救伤员。
ctx.en: After the earthquake, rescuers went all out to save the injured.

ctx.s: 经理问：“这个项目下周能完成吗？”小王说：“我们会{全力以赴}的。”
ctx.en: The manager asked, "Can this project be finished next week?" Xiao Wang said, "We'll put everything into it."

ctx.s: 离高考只剩一个月了，她正在{全力以赴}地复习。
ctx.en: With only a month left before the university entrance exam, she is revising flat out.

ctx.s: 既然决定参加，就要{全力以赴}，不能马马虎虎。
ctx.en: Now that you've decided to take part, you have to go all out, not do it half-heartedly.

ctx.s: 虽然最后输了，但队员们都{全力以赴}了，观众还是给他们鼓掌。
ctx.en: Although they lost in the end, the players had given everything, and the crowd still applauded them.

bad.s: 你放心，这件事我{全力以赴}你。
bad.en: (meant: don't worry, I'll do my utmost to help you with this)
bad.why: It takes no object. Say you will go all out, or that you will go all out to help.

bad.s: 他为了不交作业，{全力以赴}地找借口。
bad.en: (meant: he tried every trick to get out of handing in his homework)
bad.why: It means wholehearted effort on a worthy task. For scheming in many ways, especially to avoid something, use the 'by every possible means' idiom.

mean: it's a deal; that's settled then
lit: one word and it is fixed

use.how: Said on its own or after 那就/咱们 to seal an agreement between people: 好，一言为定！ The other side often answers with 一言为定 too.

cue: Your friend agrees to lend you their bike next weekend if you fix its brakes first. You shake hands on it. What do you say?

ctx.s: “明天早上八点见。”“好，{一言为定}！”
ctx.en: "See you at eight tomorrow morning." "Right, it's a deal!"

ctx.s: 那就这么说好了，下周你请我吃饭，{一言为定}。
ctx.en: So that's agreed: next week you treat me to dinner. Deal.

ctx.s: 爸爸说：“你考到九十分，我就带你去海边。”儿子马上说：“{一言为定}！”
ctx.en: Dad said, "Score ninety and I'll take you to the seaside." His son said at once, "It's a deal!"

ctx.s: 咱们{一言为定}，谁也不许反悔。
ctx.en: Let's settle it here and now, and nobody is allowed to back out.

ctx.s: 两个老板握了握手，说了声“{一言为定}”，合作就这样谈成了。
ctx.en: The two bosses shook hands, said "Agreed," and the partnership was settled just like that.

ctx.s: 上次我们不是说好了“{一言为定}”吗？你怎么又变卦了？
ctx.en: Didn't we say last time it was a deal? Why have you changed your mind again?

bad.s: 这件事我还要考虑一下，{一言为定}。
bad.en: (meant: I need to think about it a bit more, then I'll decide)
bad.why: It seals an agreement right now, so it contradicts still needing time to think. Say you will reply once you have thought it over.

bad.s: 老师在课上{一言为定}地讲了语法。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher explained the grammar decisively)
bad.why: It is not an adverb for firm or clear speaking; it is only a spoken formula for sealing a deal between people.

story.text: In his book of literary criticism, Liu Xie surveyed the styles of earlier writers. Of the poet Xi Kang (Xi Shuye) he said that, being bold and gallant, his writing had lofty inspiration and blazing brilliance. The phrase first described the vigour of a writer's style and later came to mean being in high spirits.

use.how: Adverbial (兴高采烈地跑回家) or predicate (孩子们兴高采烈). Describes lively, visible joy, often of a group, at an outing, event or good news.

near.diff: 得意洋洋 is smug pride in one's own success and often criticises; 兴高采烈 is open, innocent cheerfulness.
喜出望外 is delight at unexpected good news; 兴高采烈 describes the lively, excited mood people show.

cue: On the last day of term, the children pour out of school laughing and shouting, off on their holidays. How do they look?

ctx.s: 放假了，孩子们{兴高采烈}地跑出校门。
ctx.en: School was out, and the children ran out of the gates in high spirits.

ctx.s: 他{兴高采烈}地告诉我，他找到工作了。
ctx.en: He excitedly told me he had found a job.

ctx.s: 球赛赢了，球迷们{兴高采烈}地在街上唱歌。
ctx.en: Their team had won, and the fans sang jubilantly in the streets.

ctx.s: 看大家{兴高采烈}的样子，今天一定有什么好事吧？
ctx.en: Everyone looks so cheerful; something good must have happened today?

ctx.s: 一家人{兴高采烈}地去郊游，没想到半路下起了大雨。
ctx.en: The family set off happily on an outing, but it started pouring halfway there.

ctx.s: 晚会上，同学们{兴高采烈}，又唱又跳，一直玩到深夜。
ctx.en: At the party the classmates were in great spirits, singing and dancing late into the night.

bad.s: 他安静地坐在窗前，{兴高采烈}地看书。
bad.en: (meant: he sat quietly by the window, happily reading)
bad.why: It describes lively, visible excitement, which clashes with sitting quietly. For relish in reading, use the 'with keen interest' idiom.

bad.s: 他考了第一名，就{兴高采烈}地看不起别人。
bad.en: (meant: after coming first he proudly looked down on others)
bad.why: Looking down on others is smug self-satisfaction, a different idiom. This one is innocent cheerfulness with no contempt in it.

mean: with great relish or keen interest

use.how: After 得 or before a verb with 地, with 吃, 看, 听, 讲: 吃得津津有味, 津津有味地看. Describes a person relishing food or absorbed in a story or book.

near.diff: 狼吞虎咽 is eating fast and greedily; 津津有味 is eating slowly enough to savour and enjoy it.
全神贯注 is total concentration, even on dull work; 津津有味 says the person is enjoying it.

cue: Your grandfather spends the whole afternoon with an old adventure novel, chuckling and savouring every page. How is he reading?

ctx.s: 弟弟{津津有味}地吃着妈妈做的饺子。
ctx.en: My little brother is tucking into the dumplings Mum made, enjoying every bite.

ctx.s: 这本小说我看得{津津有味}，一个晚上就看完了。
ctx.en: I enjoyed this novel so much that I finished it in one evening.

ctx.s: 爷爷讲起年轻时的故事，孩子们听得{津津有味}。
ctx.en: When Grandpa told stories from his youth, the children listened, enthralled.

ctx.s: 这道菜看起来很普通，他却吃得{津津有味}，连说好吃。
ctx.en: The dish looked ordinary, but he ate it with relish, saying again and again how good it was.

ctx.s: 你在看什么，看得这么{津津有味}？
ctx.en: What are you reading that's got you so absorbed?

ctx.s: 别人觉得历史课很无聊，她却学得{津津有味}。
ctx.en: Others find history lessons boring, but she studies the subject with real relish.

bad.s: 我饿坏了，{津津有味}地三分钟就吃完了一大碗面。
bad.en: (meant: I was starving and wolfed down a big bowl of noodles in three minutes)
bad.why: Eating fast out of hunger is wolfing food down, a different idiom. This one means savouring the food with pleasure.

bad.s: 这个苹果很{津津有味}。
bad.en: (meant: this apple tastes very good)
bad.why: It describes how a person eats, reads or listens, not how the food tastes, and it does not take 'very'. Just say the apple is delicious.
